hero.headline: Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties face potential $283 million in losses from property tax referendum
hero.teaser: A Florida property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption could cost Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties hundreds of millions of dollars starting in 2027.
hero.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of the new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties offered estimates of the potential losses. Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County faces $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County faces $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if there is a cut in property taxes, there will be real shortfalls and real challenges. Revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are a possibility, but officials do not know if it will be an increase in sales tax or user fees for other services.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said he is happy there is a proposal out to the voters and they can make a decision with it. He said this is more of a break for the struggling family in a $300,000 home working several jobs to make sure ends meet.

cards.headline: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaks out after receiving death threats
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds received death threats as he campaigns for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. Donalds, a Naples Republican in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized rather than treated as human beings. He said that when demonization reaches certain levels, it gives an opening to somebody who has real mental health issues to try to do something crazy. While Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it as their responsibility to take somebody else's life. Despite the threats, Donalds said the incidents strengthened his resolve to work hard to be the state's next governor and keep Florida free. He is undeterred and promising to keep going, expressing confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island Erosion Could Split Island at Peck Lake, State Report Warns
cards.teaser: A state report warns that erosion has become so severe along Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline that the ocean could breach at Peck Lake and split the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater.

Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. According to Perry, over 33 threatened and endangered species live in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year, describing the effort as "reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over."

cards.headline: Florida Voters Split on Property Tax Ballot Measure Going to November Vote
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to raise the homestead exemption and roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure would need 60 percent approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Brian Edington said he supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. "I think it's a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners," Edington said. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his own neighborhood trash collection as an example. "I have trash services in my neighborhood, they pick it up twice, I don't need it twice a week, once a week would be adequate," Edington said. Rosabella Olivares expressed concern about reduced funding. "There's going to be less money because everything is expensive now," Olivares said. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed more skepticism. One renter along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach them. "Pretty sure they're going to raise the rent on everybody, all the renters, I'm pretty sure they're going to raise those taxes," the renter said.

cards.headline: Florida May Ban Fourth of July Fireworks Due to Severe Drought Conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are weighing a ban on fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence as Florida faces drought conditions more severe than 1998.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders monitor drought conditions to determine whether to ban fireworks for the nation's 250th anniversary. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services reports that this year's drought is more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented. The entire state is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about a potential ban. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said in May. He acknowledged the significance of the 250th celebration but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, the store has experienced increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Manager Bill Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions closely but remains cautiously optimistic, noting "there's plenty of rain in the forecast." The Department of Agriculture indicated a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River Counties Fertilizer Ban Takes Effect June 1
cards.teaser: Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St.
cards.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns or landscaping. The ban is designed to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season that can cause algae blooms in local waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County said the ban protects these waterways from harmful algae. According to Skaggs, algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants needed by fish and wildlife, and at certain densities harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, said composting offers a practical alternative during the ban for gardens and landscaping. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape."

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban takes effect in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties through September
cards.teaser: A ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen is now in effect across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties through September 30 to reduce harmful algae blooms during rainy season.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen through September 30. According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban aims to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Harmful algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants needed by fish and wildlife. At certain densities, these blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an alternative during the ban. He said composting can work like a small trash can and is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscapes and gardens.

hero.headline: 35 Foster Youth Graduate at ChildNet Celebration at Palm Beach State College
hero.teaser: ChildNet held its annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, honoring 35 foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
hero.body:
ChildNet, a nonprofit serving foster youth in Broward and Palm Beach counties, celebrated a significant milestone as 35 students graduated at an annual ceremony held at Palm Beach State College. The event recognized young adults who have received support from the organization through education, adoption services, and independent living resources. The graduates represent foster youth and young adults who have worked toward stability and success while navigating the challenges of the child welfare system.

Among those celebrating their accomplishments were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, two graduates who both experienced the loss of a parent and turned to ChildNet for guidance and support. The organization provided them with essential resources to help them move forward during difficult times. Diaz addressed her peers with an encouraging message about perseverance. She told others in similar situations to believe in their potential, work hard, and stay committed to their education and dreams. She emphasized the importance of pushing through pain and continuing to try despite obstacles. Saintfort shared similar advice, urging others to maintain faith in their ability to succeed.

Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, spoke about the meaning of the celebration. He acknowledged that the evening represented the combined efforts of the entire community, including case workers from ChildNet and the Department of Children and Family Services, as well as the determination of the graduates themselves. Rein emphasized that the event was primarily a chance to recognize and celebrate the hard work and resilience demonstrated by these young adults.

Both graduates have already begun planning their futures. Diaz has enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with aspirations of becoming a doctor. Saintfort is pursuing a vocational program to become a plumber. Their plans reflect the diverse paths these young adults are taking as they transition to independence and build careers. The graduation celebration highlighted not only the individual achievements of these 35 students but also the critical role that organizations like ChildNet play in supporting vulnerable youth through education and life skills training.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Rental Assistance Program Overwhelmed by Demand
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but its Emergency Rental Assistance Program has only $2 million in grant funding available.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program is overwhelmed by demand each month. The Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding available, but applications fill within hours of opening. Program director Dr. James Green explained that the county receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance monthly and currently has about 800 applications in queue. Typically, about 600 applications come in within the first couple hours after the portal opens. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Green urged anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

Rising costs of living have driven the surge in applications. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa after 12 years working as an educator, switched to real estate to afford rent. "Almost every day, all the bills are rising except our paychecks," she said. For those unable to access the county program, 211 offers 24/7 assistance and connects residents with nonprofits and other area assistance programs.

cards.headline: Florida Shark Dive Operators Fight Federal Feeding Ban
cards.teaser: A federal bill that would ban shark feeding in waters within 200 miles of Florida is drawing criticism from shark diving operators who say it unfairly targets their conservation work.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters call it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators argues the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives. This practice is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Campbell emphasized that Congress has not yet asked the industry to present data or explain their practices.

Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members point to Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as a cautionary example, noting that shark incidents and fatalities have increased since the ban was enacted. According to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. In a letter to Congress, Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders including both tourism operators and fisheries in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces threat of breach at Peck Lake as erosion threatens to split barrier island
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that erosion could cause the ocean to break through at Peck Lake on Jupiter Island, potentially splitting the 11.5-mile barrier island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The report found nearly the entire coastline is critically eroded, threatening roads, buildings, drainage systems, natural habitats, wildlife and ancient sites. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater to survive. The consequences extend well beyond the shoreline, with the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, at risk. Wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are also threatened. Perry noted there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in all of those areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town fights erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. He acknowledged the town is "reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over" and will continue doing so as long as there is money. Field warned that if funding for beach renourishment in Florida goes away, the coastline of Florida will change very quickly.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard says she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024.
cards.body:
A woman from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. Mary Hubbard says she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident in June 2024, when she purchased the SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages.

According to the complaint, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. She documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product. The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, and Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed with 8,000 monthly calls for help
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County receives about 600 applications in the first couple hours they open for emergency rental assistance each month, with 800 applications currently in the queue.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, designed to help residents who can't pay rent. However, demand far outweighs available funds each month. Dr. James Green, program director, said there are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on data combined with 211. The county currently has about 800 applications in the queue for rental assistance, with typically 600 applications received in the first couple of hours after applications open at the beginning of each month. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Green urges anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living including housing, gas, and food. For those who cannot get into the county's program, 211 is another important option available 24/7 that connects residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax proposal ahead of November ballot
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

Brian Edington said he supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. He said he is comfortable with local governments having to spend less and pointed to his own neighborhood's trash services as an example of where cuts could be made, noting that twice-weekly pickup could be reduced to once weekly. However, another resident identified as Stan said he does not want funding eliminated entirely, citing the importance of infrastructure. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed more skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach renters and predicted landlords would raise rent on everybody. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about what reduced funding could mean, saying "There's going to be less money ... because everything is expensive now."

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.body:
Demolition of the Indian River Mall began this week as crews started removing the Macy's building and the former Sears location. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager overseeing the redevelopment, said the work represents the first phase of the revitalization project.

Community members gathered in the mall's parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra, a nearby resident, expressed support for the project, saying "To be honest, I'm really happy they're tearing this down." Mark Manera from Vero Beach, who has frequented the mall for years, described it as looking "like the death of a beautiful building" and noted "It was more like a graveyard" due to a "steady decline year after year after year." Despite his sadness, Manera said change is needed, adding "If that brings new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful."

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center spanning around 300,000 square feet with retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces. He described the vision as "a city within a city," replacing what had been "a dead mall for the last 12 years." Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, though the team continues working on permitting for the remaining project phases.

hero.headline: 100 paddlers to cross 80 miles of Atlantic from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach for cystic fibrosis fundraiser
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling across the open Atlantic Ocean.
hero.body:
The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis will bring more than 100 paddlers across 80 miles of the Atlantic Ocean from Bimini, Bahamas, to Lake Worth Beach on June 13. Participants launch at midnight and are expected to arrive after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, established by event founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held.

Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Broadway's 'Beetlejuice' musical runs through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
cards.body:
Broadway's "Beetlejuice" musical has landed at the Kravis Center's Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, running through June 7. The production brings Tim Burton's 1988 film to life on stage with spooky humor and over-the-top visuals. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon in the iconic striped suit. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger told WPTV. He noted that Keaton appears in the film for only 15 minutes. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and the demon Beetlejuice.

Stajmiger said one of his favorite aspects of performing is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with the audience and share moments with them. Early in the run, an unexpected moment occurred during a wig change when both wigs came off simultaneously, leaving him bald for an entire scene. Rather than letting the mishap disrupt his performance, Stajmiger played with the moment. Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 and can be purchased at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker enters race for CD 11
hero.teaser: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker launched a campaign to succeed retiring U.S. Representative Daniel Webster in Florida's 11th Congressional District.
hero.body:
Carey Baker, 63, a lifelong Eustis resident and former Lake County Property Appraiser, is running for Congress in Florida's 11th Congressional District. He will face Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini in the Republican primary. Sabatini, once considered Baker's protégé, has already run for the seat previously.

Baker represented much of Central Florida in the state legislature, serving in both the House and Senate before winning election as a constitutional officer. He was first elected to the Florida House in 2000 and later advanced to the Senate. His father also served the area in the Florida House. Most recently, Baker spent multiple terms as Lake County Property Appraiser before losing his re-election bid in 2024. He had filed as a write-in candidate but was defeated by Republican David Jordan by a three-to-one margin in the general election. Despite the loss, Baker's campaign raised $233,000, demonstrating the fundraising ability that will be critical in the primary race. After his defeat, Baker worked unsuccessfully with Sabatini in an effort to become Lake County Republican Party Chair.

The 11th Congressional District encompasses all of Sumter County, portions of western Orange County, and most of Lake County following the latest congressional redistricting. The district leans heavily Republican, with more than 57 percent of voters supporting President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, making it likely to remain in Republican hands in the general election.

On the Democratic side, repeat candidate Barbie Harden Hall announced on Saturday that she was suspending her campaign due to health issues. Hall had been the leading fundraiser among Democrats and appeared to be the frontrunner for the party's nomination for the second consecutive election cycle. Three other Democratic candidates remain in the race: Royal Webster, Shawn Bettis, and Dan Williams.

cards.headline: Tampa City Council chair pushes to delay Rays CRA vote amid unresolved stadium negotiations
cards.teaser: Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin is seeking to postpone a Community Redevelopment Agency discussion tied to the Tampa Bay Rays stadium proposal until at least July.
cards.body:
Tampa City Council Chair Alan Clendenin submitted a memo requesting that the Rays Community Redevelopment Agency discussion be deferred until at least July, and possibly longer, rather than being taken up by the Tampa CRA as originally planned. Clendenin said the issue is not ready for a vote as negotiations continue. The Rays stadium MOU approved by Tampa and Hillsborough County last month includes $80 million from the city of Tampa and another $100 million tied to the Tampa CRA, in addition to other public dollars. Clendenin also cited recent uncertainty over property tax reform as another factor for negotiators to consider.

Clendenin sharply disputed Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal's characterization of where negotiations stand, clarifying that behind-the-scenes talks are still ongoing. He said the earlier votes by the City Council and County Commission represented support for the general direction of the non-binding MOU, but not final approval of the CRA terms. Several options remain on the table for the CRA-related portion of the deal, including not using the CRA, creating a different type of district, or using another special district structure. For the CRA portion, nothing has been agreed to by any party, Clendenin said. He defended keeping negotiation details confidential, stating that you don't negotiate the deal out in public.

cards.headline: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds speaks out after receiving death threats
cards.teaser: Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds received death threats as he campaigns for the Republican nomination in the August primary.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. Donalds, a Naples Republican in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after re-sharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the Governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized rather than treated as human beings. He said that when demonization reaches certain levels, it gives an opening to somebody who has real mental health issues to try to do something crazy. While Donalds considers himself a free speech absolutist, he stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it as their responsibility to take somebody else's life. Despite the threats, Donalds said the incidents strengthened his resolve to work hard to be the state's next governor and keep Florida free. He is undeterred and promising to keep going, expressing confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second campaign for Jacksonville's HD 12
cards.teaser: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin filed for a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago.
cards.body:
The 22-year-old repeat candidate filed for the House race Friday, just three days before the beginning of qualifying on Monday, June 8. Sandlin lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. He said the Florida Democratic Party and he had been talking and that they agreed that this seat was just too close in 24 to leave uncontested. Sandlin had filed for the race to succeed Democrat Jimmy Peluso in City Council District 7, but has dropped that race. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, it is likely Sandlin will advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is running in HD 12 to succeed Duggan. Freeman is well-positioned for his Primary, having raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee, For the Future We Want, through the end of May. He had roughly $390,000 on hand at the end of last month. Freeman was appointed to the Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Gov. Rick Scott to fill a vacancy. He was then elected to an at-large, countywide seat twice in 2019 and 2023, and served a year as Council President. He has already announced that he will resign from the Council once a replacement is elected, which could be as soon as August, as there is a Special Election for the seat.

cards.headline: Cuba's former President Raúl Castro makes first public appearance since U.S. indictment
cards.teaser: Raúl Castro appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft.
cards.body:
Raúl Castro, Cuba's low-profile former president and revolutionary guerrilla, appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft. Castro's celebration of his 95th birthday with top officials and military leaders at the Ministry of Interior in Havana on late Friday offered Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to close ranks and project defiance as the Trump administration escalates its pressure campaign on the fuel-starved island. State TV broadcast footage of Castro, clad in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater to a standing ovation, followed by his grandson and bodyguard, Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez, and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel.

Díaz-Canel delivered an effusive tribute to the "heroism and dignity" displayed by Castro and his late brother, Fidel Castro, the central figure of the Cuban revolution. He praised Raúl Castro, who served as defense minister of Cuba for nearly 50 years, for his "courage and loyalty (that) made him a target from a very early age for the intelligence services of our enemies." Although he formally retired from politics in April 2021, Castro is believed to wield considerable political power. The Justice Department's indictment unsealed in May accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.

cards.headline: Senator Rick Scott honors father's D-Day service in World War II
cards.teaser: Senator Rick Scott marked the anniversary of D-Day by remembering his father's service during the 1944 World War II military operation in Normandy.
cards.body:
On Saturday, Naples Republican and Navy veteran Senator Rick Scott honored the memory of World War II by remembering D-Day, the famous 1944 military operation in which more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy to begin the liberation of German-occupied France. Orba Scott, who raised the Senator, was among those who participated in the operation. According to Senator Scott, his adopted father parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

Senator Scott acknowledged that while his father was blessed to return home from battle, many brave individuals made the ultimate sacrifice in defense of freedom and did not return home. As a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, Scott vowed to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. He stated that he is fighting every day to improve the military, take care of the nation's veterans, and protect the legacy so the next generation knows and appreciates the sacrifices made for their freedoms.

hero.headline: Dolphins in Indian River Lagoon face increasing entanglement threat from fishing line
hero.teaser: Wildlife scientists report a skyrocketing number of dolphins entangled in fishing line in the Indian River Lagoon.
hero.body:
Wildlife scientists have raised alarms about a sharp rise in dolphin entanglement cases involving fishing line in the Indian River Lagoon. The escalating incidents represent a growing environmental concern for the region's marine mammal population. Researchers monitoring the situation say the trend reflects a troubling pattern that demands immediate attention from both the scientific community and the public.

The Indian River Lagoon stretches across multiple counties along Florida's east coast, making it an important habitat for dolphins and other wildlife. As entanglement cases continue to climb, experts are working to understand the scope of the problem and identify solutions. These entanglements pose serious health risks to dolphins, potentially causing injury, infection, or death if the animals become trapped in discarded or improperly disposed fishing gear.

Beyond the immediate threat of fishing line entanglement, the lagoon faces broader environmental pressures that compound the challenges facing dolphins and other marine life. The region experiences significant nutrient runoff during the rainy season, which can trigger harmful algae blooms in waterways like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. According to environmental officials, these blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms may release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health, and overall ecosystem health.

Recognizing these interconnected threats, local governments have implemented protective measures. Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties established a fertilizer ban running from June 1 through September 30 each year, prohibiting fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen during the peak rainy season. Environmental officials say this restriction helps reduce nutrient runoff that contributes to algae blooms. Residents and property managers are encouraged to use composting as an alternative method for adding nutrients to landscaping during the ban period. Wildlife scientists continue monitoring dolphin populations in the lagoon while advocating for practices that protect both marine mammals and the broader ecosystem. The combination of reducing water pollution and addressing fishing line hazards represents a comprehensive approach to safeguarding the Indian River Lagoon's vulnerable dolphin population.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
cards.teaser: Indian River, Martin and St.
cards.body:
Starting June 30, Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will ban fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen during the rainy season. The seasonal restriction applies to all lawn and landscaping fertilizer use across the three counties.

Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban aims to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that causes algae blooms in local waterways like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. According to Skaggs, these blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins affecting human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommended composting as an alternative during the ban for gardens and landscaping. Ricketts said a small trash can provides the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to your landscape.

cards.body:

The Indian River Lagoon is home to a resident dolphin population. Wildlife experts are tracking the increase in entanglement incidents affecting the marine mammals.
